CHAPTER 01 · MEET AI7
LESSON 1.1Meet AI

What is artificial intelligence?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of computing that develops systems able to perform tasks such as recognizing speech, identifying objects and generating text. A calculator follows exact arithmetic rules. A speech recognition system, by contrast, can learn patterns from many recordings to recognize unfamiliar voices. Not every digital device uses AI.

LOOK CLOSER
🧮CalculatorFixed rulesNOT AI
🎙️Voice assistantLearns from recordingsAI
⏰Alarm clockFixed timeNOT AI
📺Video suggestionsLearns what you likeAI
📱
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A phone can recognize spoken words even when two people pronounce them differently.

🔑 KEY WORDArtificial intelligence

A field of computing that builds systems able to recognize speech, identify objects or generate text.

CHAPTER 01 · MEET AI8
LESSON 1.2Meet AI

A short history of AI

In 1950, Alan Turing proposed a way to discuss whether machines could imitate human conversation. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop helped establish AI as a research field. Early systems often used rules written by people. Later, larger datasets and faster computers made machine learning more useful. Today, generative AI can produce text, images and other media.

HOW IT WORKS
📏
RulesSTEP 1
➜
📚
LearningSTEP 2
➜
🎨
GenerationSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
1950Alan Turing asks: can a machine imitate a conversation?
1956Dartmouth workshop: AI becomes a research field
Early AIRules written by people
LaterBig datasets + fast computers: machine learning
TodayGenerative AI makes text, images and media
♟️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A chess program may search possible moves, while a modern image generator learns visual patterns.

🔑 KEY WORDGenerative AI

AI that produces new text, images or other media.

CHAPTER 01 · MEET AI9
LESSON 1.3Meet AI

AI is not a human brain

Most AI today is designed for particular tasks. A model that recognizes pictures cannot automatically repair a bicycle. Generative models can produce convincing language without having human experiences or reliable knowledge of every fact. People decide how systems are built, tested and used.

HOW IT WORKS
🎯
Human goalSTEP 1
➜
🔮
Machine predictionSTEP 2
➜
🙋
Human decisionSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🤖 AI is good atSpotting patterns in huge dataPredicting what comes nextMaking a fast first draft
🙋 Only peopleHaving real experiencesDeciding what mattersTaking responsibility
🗺️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A navigation app may predict traffic but cannot decide what matters most to your family.

🔑 KEY WORDPrediction

An AI's best estimate based on patterns. It is not a fact, and it is not a decision.

⭐ Remember
  1. Not every digital device uses AI: AI learns patterns, a calculator follows fixed rules.
  2. AI moved from rules written by people, to learning from data, to generating new media.
  3. AI predicts. People set the goals and make the decisions.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Name one device that uses AI and one that does not. Explain the difference.
  2. What changed between early rule-based AI and machine learning?
  3. A navigation app predicts traffic. Which decision should stay yours?

CHAPTER 02 · SAFE AND RESPONSIBLE AI11
LESSON 2.1Safe and Responsible AI

Your digital footprint

A digital footprint is the information left behind when people use online services. Names, addresses, school schedules and photos can reveal more than expected. AI services may process information on remote computers. Before sharing anything, check school rules and ask a trusted adult when unsure.

HOW IT WORKS
🪪
Personal dataSTEP 1
➜
🔍
Privacy checkSTEP 2
➜
✅
Safe exampleSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🛑 Keep it private🏠Home address📸Photos of faces🔑Passwords🗓️Where you are, when
👍 OK to use🦸A fictional name📚A school subject⚽A hobby❓A general question
📅
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

Use a fictional student name when asking AI to create a sample timetable.

🔑 KEY WORDDigital footprint

The information left behind when people use online services.

CHAPTER 02 · SAFE AND RESPONSIBLE AI12
LESSON 2.2Safe and Responsible AI

Fairness and bias

Bias is a tendency that can produce unfair results. AI may learn patterns from examples that do not represent everyone equally. Fairness requires careful choices about data, testing and how decisions are made. A person should be able to question important automated decisions.

HOW IT WORKS
🗂️
Training examplesSTEP 1
➜
🤖
ModelSTEP 2
➜
⚖️
Fairness reviewSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
Unbalanced training data
Mostly one group: the model may work worse for the others.
Balanced training data
Everyone is represented: a fairer start (still test it!).
🗣️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A speech system trained mostly on one accent may struggle with other accents.

🔑 KEY WORDBias

A tendency that can produce unfair results.

CHAPTER 02 · SAFE AND RESPONSIBLE AI13
LESSON 2.3Safe and Responsible AI

Digital identity and consent

AI can imitate voices and create realistic pictures. A synthetic image is not proof that an event happened. Consent means permission: do not copy another person’s face or voice without appropriate permission. Respect creators by checking licenses and acknowledging sources.

HOW IT WORKS
🎨
CreateSTEP 1
➜
🙋
Check permissionSTEP 2
➜
📤
Share responsiblySTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🙋✓ They said yesAsk before using a face or a voice
🏷️✓ It is labeledSay clearly: “made with AI”
🙏✓ Creators creditedCheck licenses, name your sources
🦊
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A fictional mascot is a safer choice for a school advertisement than copying a classmate’s face.

🔑 KEY WORDConsent

Permission. You need it before you use another person's face or voice.

⭐ Remember
  1. Your digital footprint can reveal more than you expect: share less, and use fictional names.
  2. AI can be unfair when its training examples do not represent everyone.
  3. Consent means permission: never copy someone's face or voice without it.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Which three details should you never share with an AI app?
  2. Explain how bias can enter an AI system. Give an example.
  3. A friend wants to make an AI video with a teacher's face. What must happen first?

CHAPTER 03 · HOW AI LEARNS15
LESSON 3.1How AI Learns

Learning from examples

Machine learning is a way of building systems that improve at a task by finding patterns in data. In supervised learning, examples have labels. A model might see pictures labeled pencil, notebook or eraser. During training, it adjusts internal numerical settings so its predictions better match the labels.

HOW IT WORKS
🏷️
Labeled examplesSTEP 1
➜

TrainingSTEP 2
➜

label: pencil
📒📒📒📒
label: notebook
🧽🧽🧽🧽
label: eraser
→
🤖Modeladjusts its settings
✏️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A model trained only on yellow pencils may struggle with a blue pencil.

🔑 KEY WORDLabel

The correct answer attached to a training example, such as “pencil”.

CHAPTER 03 · HOW AI LEARNS16
LESSON 3.2How AI Learns

Neural networks and deep learning

A neural network is a mathematical system made of connected processing units. Each unit combines numbers and passes a result onward. Networks with many layers can learn complex patterns; this is called deep learning. In image recognition, early layers may respond to edges, while later layers combine patterns into more complex features.

HOW IT WORKS
🟦
PixelsSTEP 1
➜
🧠
Feature layersSTEP 2
➜
🚲
Object scoreSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🚲
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

Recognizing a bicycle may involve patterns associated with wheels, frames and handlebars.

🔑 KEY WORDNeural network

A mathematical system of connected units. With many layers, it is called deep learning.

CHAPTER 03 · HOW AI LEARNS17
LESSON 3.3How AI Learns

Testing and confidence

Testing uses examples that were not used to train the model. Accuracy is the proportion of correct predictions on a test set. A confidence score is a model’s estimate, not a guarantee. Lighting, backgrounds and unusual objects can change results. A useful model needs varied examples and honest evaluation.

HOW IT WORKS
🖼️
New imageSTEP 1
➜
🤔
PredictionSTEP 2
➜
✔️
Compare with truthSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✓✗✗
18 ÷ 20= 0.9 = 90%accuracy on this test
💯
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

If 18 out of 20 test pictures are classified correctly, accuracy is 90 percent on that test.

🔑 KEY WORDAccuracy

The proportion of correct predictions on a test set.

⭐ Remember
  1. Supervised learning uses labeled examples to adjust a model's settings.
  2. Deep learning stacks many layers that combine simple patterns into complex ones.
  3. Always test with new examples: accuracy and confidence are estimates, not guarantees.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Why must test pictures be different from training pictures?
  2. A model only saw yellow pencils. What could go wrong, and how would you fix it?
  3. A model got 15 out of 20 test pictures right. What is its accuracy?

LESSON 4.1Become a Prompt Engineer

How language models generate text

A language model processes text as small units called tokens. It learns statistical patterns from large collections of text and generates responses by predicting tokens in context. This can produce useful explanations, but a fluent sentence is not necessarily a true sentence.

The words after “Once upon a” are likely to include “time”, although other continuations are possible.

🔑 KEY WORDToken

A small unit of text that a language model processes.

CHAPTER 04 · BECOME A PROMPT ENGINEER20
LESSON 4.2Become a Prompt Engineer

The anatomy of a prompt

A prompt is an instruction or question given to an AI system. A useful prompt often specifies a role, task, context and output format. Context helps the model understand the audience and constraints. Clear instructions reduce ambiguity but cannot guarantee accuracy.

HOW IT WORKS
🎭
Role + taskSTEP 1
➜
🧭
ContextSTEP 2
➜

LOOK CLOSER

⚽
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

Ask for a five-day football practice plan for a beginner, with 20-minute sessions and a table.

🔑 KEY WORDPrompt

An instruction or question given to an AI system.

CHAPTER 04 · BECOME A PROMPT ENGINEER21
LESSON 4.3Become a Prompt Engineer

Iteration and human judgment

Iteration means improving something through repeated attempts. A first AI answer is a draft. Read it, identify missing details and ask for a specific change. Verify facts and adapt the result to your own goals. Prompt engineering is not a magic phrase; it is clear communication and evaluation.

HOW IT WORKS
📝
DraftSTEP 1
➜
🗣️
FeedbackSTEP 2
➜
✨
Revised draftSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
DRAFTStudy 2 hours a dayHard exam questions
MY FEEDBACK“Make the sessions 20 minutes, with simpler examples.”
REVISED ✨Study 20 minutes a daySimple examples first
📚
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

If a study plan is too difficult, request shorter sessions and simpler examples.

🔑 KEY WORDIteration

Improving something through repeated attempts.

⭐ Remember
  1. A language model predicts tokens: a fluent sentence is not always a true one.
  2. A strong prompt gives a role, a task, context and an output format.
  3. The first answer is a draft: give feedback, then verify.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Write a prompt with all four parts for a topic you like.
  2. Why can a very clear prompt still produce a wrong answer?
  3. An AI study plan is too hard for you. Write the follow-up you would send.

CHAPTER 05 · AI CAN BE WRONG23
LESSON 5.1AI Can Be Wrong

Why confident answers can be false

Generative AI can produce a statement that sounds correct but is unsupported or false. This is often called a hallucination. A model may combine patterns into an invented fact, citation or name. It may also lack current information. Confidence in wording is not evidence.

HOW IT WORKS
💬
ClaimSTEP 1
➜
🔎
Evidence checkSTEP 2
➜
✅
ConclusionSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🤖

For your project, read “The Secret Science of Clouds” by Dr. Nora Vale, published in 2019. It is the best book on this topic.

🔎 Library catalog: no record🔎 Publisher list: no recordINVENTED!

A made-up example: the title and the author sound real, but they do not exist.

📕
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

An AI might invent a book title that sounds like a real science textbook.

🔑 KEY WORDHallucination

A confident AI statement that is unsupported or false.

CHAPTER 05 · AI CAN BE WRONG24
LESSON 5.2AI Can Be Wrong

Sources and evidence

A reliable source has relevant expertise, clear evidence and a traceable origin. A primary source provides direct evidence, while a secondary source interprets it. Check the date and compare independent sources. Two websites repeating the same rumor do not count as independent confirmation.

HOW IT WORKS
📰
SourceSTEP 1
➜
📅
Date and evidenceSTEP 2
➜
🔁
Cross-checkSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🏫
Official school announcementPrimary, traceable, dated
📰
News article that quotes itSecondary
📲
Forwarded message, no authorUnknown origin
🏫
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

For a school holiday, the official school announcement is stronger evidence than a forwarded message.

🔑 KEY WORDPrimary source

A source that gives direct evidence. A secondary source interprets it.

CHAPTER 05 · AI CAN BE WRONG25
LESSON 5.3AI Can Be Wrong

Images, misinformation and context

A real photograph can be misleading if it is cropped or given a false caption. AI-generated images can also look realistic. Visual clues alone cannot prove authenticity. Look for the original source and supporting evidence before sharing.

HOW IT WORKS
🖼️
ImageSTEP 1
➜
🗺️
Original contextSTEP 2
➜
✅
Verified storySTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
🌊🏠🌊
“TODAY: our street is flooded!”
→
🔍 Find the original📅 Taken years ago📍 In another city✅ Real photo, false caption
🌊
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A photograph of flooding from a different year may be shared as if it happened today.

🔑 KEY WORDMisinformation

False or misleading information, such as a real photo with a false caption.

⭐ Remember
  1. A hallucination sounds confident but is unsupported or false.
  2. Reliable sources have expertise, evidence, a traceable origin and a date.
  3. A real photo can mislead with a false caption: find its original context.
✏️ Quick review
  1. What is a hallucination? Give an example.
  2. Why do two websites repeating a rumor not count as independent confirmation?
  3. Before you share a shocking photo, which two things do you check?

LESSON 6.1AI Media Studio

How digital images are made

Digital images consist of pixels, tiny colored elements arranged in a grid. Some generative image systems learn to turn random noise into an image guided by a text description. The result is newly generated media, not necessarily a photograph of a real object.

🎒
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

An AI can create a picture of a backpack that does not exist in any shop.

🔑 KEY WORDPixel

A tiny colored element in the grid that makes up a digital image.

CHAPTER 06 · AI MEDIA STUDIO28
LESSON 6.2AI Media Studio

Sound and synthetic voices

Sound is vibration. Digital audio represents sound through measurements taken many times per second. Text-to-speech systems turn written words into spoken audio, using learned patterns of pronunciation and rhythm. Synthetic voices should be used transparently and with appropriate permission.

A school video can use a fictional narrator rather than imitate a real teacher.

🔑 KEY WORDText-to-speech

A system that turns written words into spoken audio.

CHAPTER 06 · AI MEDIA STUDIO29
LESSON 6.3AI Media Studio

Visual storytelling and advertising

A storyboard plans a sequence of scenes before production. A commercial often introduces a problem, presents a product, shows its benefit and ends with a call to action. Color, framing, music and pacing affect how viewers feel. Responsible advertising avoids false promises.

HOW IT WORKS

EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A reusable bottle advertisement can show a thirsty student, the bottle, refilling and a final message.

🔑 KEY WORDStoryboard

A plan of a video's scenes, made before production.

⭐ Remember
  1. Images are grids of pixels; some models turn noise into an image guided by text.
  2. Text-to-speech turns a script into audio. Use synthetic voices openly and with permission.
  3. A commercial goes problem → product → benefit → call to action, with no false promises.

CHAPTER 07 · ALGORITHMS AND CODING31
LESSON 7.1Algorithms and Coding

Algorithms are instructions

An algorithm is an ordered method for solving a problem. It can be written in ordinary language, a flowchart or code. A sequence executes steps in order. A condition chooses a path based on a test. A loop repeats steps. These ideas appear in everyday routines and software.

HOW IT WORKS
🌡️
InputSTEP 1
➜

CHAPTER 07 · ALGORITHMS AND CODING32
LESSON 7.2Algorithms and Coding

From instructions to programs

Programming languages allow people to express instructions precisely. Variables store values, such as temperature. Comparisons test values, and functions group reusable instructions. Computers execute the instructions they receive, even when the programmer intended something different.

HOW IT WORKS
🌡️
TemperatureSTEP 1
➜
⚖️
Compare to 30STEP 2
➜
🌀
Fan stateSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
temperature = 31
if temperature > 30:
    fan = "ON"
else:
    fan = "OFF"
🌀
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

If temperature is above 30 degrees, turn on the fan; otherwise leave it off.

🔑 KEY WORDVariable

A named place that stores a value, such as temperature.

CHAPTER 07 · ALGORITHMS AND CODING33
LESSON 7.3Algorithms and Coding

Debugging and automation

A bug is an error that causes unexpected behavior. Debugging means finding and correcting its cause. Test normal cases, boundary cases and unusual inputs. Automation follows programmed rules; AI may instead use learned predictions. Many useful systems combine both.

HOW IT WORKS
🎯
Expected resultSTEP 1
➜
🐞
Actual resultSTEP 2
➜
🔧
Fix and retestSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
Test inputExpectedActual (rule: above 30)Result
29°COFFOFF✅
30°C?OFF🤔 Is this what we wanted?
31°CONON✅
🧪
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

Test a fan rule at 29, 30 and 31 degrees to see what happens at the boundary.

🔑 KEY WORDBug

An error that causes unexpected behavior.

⭐ Remember
  1. An algorithm is an ordered method built from sequences, conditions and loops.
  2. Variables store values and comparisons test them. Computers do exactly what they are told.
  3. A bug causes unexpected behavior: test normal, boundary and unusual cases.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Describe an everyday routine that uses a sequence, a condition and a loop.
  2. The rule says “above 30”. What does the fan do at exactly 30 degrees?
  3. What is the difference between automation and AI?

CHAPTER 08 · REINVENT THE SCHOOL: DISCOVER35
LESSON 8.1Reinvent the School: Discover

Innovation starts with people

Innovation is a useful new or improved way of doing something. It begins with understanding people’s needs rather than choosing a technology first. Observation and interviews can reveal where a process is slow, confusing or wasteful. AI is one possible tool, not always the best solution.

HOW IT WORKS

ObserveSTEP 1
➜
🤝
UnderstandSTEP 2
➜
💡
Choose a solutionSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
1👀ObserveWatch the problem happen. Count: how many, how often, how long?
2🎤InterviewAsk 3 people what is hard for them, and why.
3📝Write the need“Students need … because …”
🍽️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A crowded cafeteria may need a better queue layout rather than a complicated AI system.

🔑 KEY WORDInnovation

A useful new or improved way of doing something.

CHAPTER 08 · REINVENT THE SCHOOL: DISCOVER36
LESSON 8.2Reinvent the School: Discover

Symptoms and root causes

A symptom is a visible sign of a problem. A root cause is an underlying factor that helps explain it. Asking why several times can uncover possible causes, but evidence is needed to confirm them. Different causes may require different solutions.

HOW IT WORKS
🤒
SymptomSTEP 1
➜
🕵️
Possible causeSTEP 2
➜
📊
EvidenceSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER

🕵️ POSSIBLE ROOT CAUSES · hidden below
Moving between classroomsNo names or labelsNo lost-and-found process
🔍 Check each one with evidence before choosing a solution
📓
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

Lost notebooks may result from moving classrooms, unclear labeling or a missing lost-and-found process.

🔑 KEY WORDRoot cause

An underlying factor that helps explain a problem.

CHAPTER 08 · REINVENT THE SCHOOL: DISCOVER37
LESSON 8.3Reinvent the School: Discover

Planning a useful project

A requirement describes what a solution must do. A success criterion describes how to tell whether it works. A risk is an uncertain event that could affect the project. A small prototype with clear priorities is often more useful than a large unfinished plan.

HOW IT WORKS
📋
RequirementsSTEP 1
➜
⚠️
RisksSTEP 2
➜
🏁
Success criteriaSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER
📋RequirementsWhat it must do

Search for a lost item

Report a found item

⚠️RiskWhat could go wrong

Real student names get shared

→ Use fictional data

🏁Success criterionHow we will know

A sample item is found in under 1 minute ⏱️

⏱️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A lost-and-found demo might need search and reporting, with a target of finding a sample item in under one minute.

🔑 KEY WORDSuccess criterion

A measurable way to tell whether a solution works.

⭐ Remember
  1. Innovation starts with people's needs, not with a technology.
  2. A symptom is what you see. A root cause explains it, and needs evidence.
  3. Requirements, risks and success criteria turn an idea into a plan.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Describe a problem in your school. Is it a symptom or a root cause?
  2. Ask “why?” three times about lost notebooks. Where do you end up?
  3. Write one success criterion you could check with a stopwatch.

How websites work

HTML describes the structure of a web page. CSS controls its appearance. JavaScript adds behavior, such as responding to a button. A browser reads these instructions and displays the page. A server may provide files or store data, but a simple prototype can run locally.

LESSON 9.3Reinvent the School: Build

Prototypes and quality assurance

A prototype is an early version used to explore an idea. Quality assurance checks whether the product meets requirements. Test cases describe inputs and expected outcomes. Feedback helps improve the next version. AI-generated code still needs review, especially before collecting personal information or publishing online.

🔑 KEY WORDPrototype

An early version used to explore an idea.

⭐ Remember
  1. UI is what you see. UX is how easy and effective it is to use.
  2. HTML is structure, CSS is appearance, JavaScript is behavior.
  3. A prototype is tested and improved into Version 2. AI code still needs review.

CHAPTER 10 · THE FUTURE OF OUR PLANET43
LESSON 10.1The Future of Our Planet

Data helps us understand Earth

Environmental data includes measurements of temperature, rainfall, energy use, waste and air quality. Sensors and satellites can collect observations across time and space. AI can help detect patterns in large datasets, but results depend on the quality of the measurements.

🌱
ActSTEP 3

8 kgFri

Mean70 ÷ 5 = 14 kg
Worst dayThursday

Example: food waste in kilograms, weighed each school day.

⚖️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A school can weigh cafeteria waste each day to understand which days produce more waste.

🔑 KEY WORDEnvironmental data

Measurements such as temperature, rainfall, energy use, waste and air quality.

CHAPTER 10 · THE FUTURE OF OUR PLANET44
LESSON 10.2The Future of Our Planet

Charts and predictions

A bar chart compares categories, while a line chart shows changes over time. A mean is the sum of values divided by their number. A prediction estimates an unknown future value. A simulation explores what might happen under stated assumptions, not what is guaranteed to happen.

HOW IT WORKS
📊
BaselineSTEP 1
➜
🔀
ScenarioSTEP 2
➜
🌍
Projected impactSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER

A projection, not a measurement: it assumes the −30% really happens.

♻️
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

If weekly waste is 70 kg, a 30 percent reduction would avoid 21 kg each week.

🔑 KEY WORDSimulation

An exploration of what might happen under stated assumptions.

CHAPTER 10 · THE FUTURE OF OUR PLANET45
LESSON 10.3The Future of Our Planet

Technology and sustainability

AI can support energy management, weather forecasting and wildlife monitoring. Computing also requires electricity, equipment and sometimes water for cooling. A responsible solution compares benefits with costs and environmental impacts. People must decide whether the technology is appropriate.

HOW IT WORKS
👍
BenefitSTEP 1
➜
🔌
Resource costSTEP 2
➜
⚖️
DecisionSTEP 3
LOOK CLOSER

Benefit

Cost

Benefit

Cost

🤖Predictive AILearns the schedule, plans heating

Benefit

Cost

Example only: more technology can bring more benefit, but it also costs more. Choose what the building needs.

💡
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

A building can reduce wasted energy with simple timers, sensors or predictive controls depending on its needs.

🔑 KEY WORDSustainability

Meeting today's needs without harming the future.

⭐ Remember
  1. Environmental data comes from measurements, and results depend on their quality.
  2. A simulation explores “what if” under stated assumptions. It is not a guarantee.
  3. Technology has costs too: compare its benefits with the resources it uses.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Waste was 12, 18 and 9 kg on three days. What is the mean?
  2. What is the difference between a measurement and a projection?
  3. Name one environmental cost of using computers and AI.

CHAPTER 11 · THE EXHIBITION49
LESSON 11.3The Exhibition

The future of work and AI

AI may change tasks in many professions, from medicine and engineering to art and education. People will still need subject knowledge, communication, creativity and judgment. Learning how to evaluate tools and adapt to new technology is more valuable than memorizing one particular application.

HOW IT WORKS

🤖
AI assistanceSTEP 2
➜
🤝
Responsible outcomeSTEP 3

🏗️Engineer

🤖 AI can help withExploring many designs fast

🙋 People stillSafety standards, choosing the solution

🎨Artist

🤖 AI can help withSketching ideas and variations

🙋 People stillThe story, the style, the meaning

👷
EVERYDAY EXAMPLE

🔑 KEY WORDAttribution

Saying clearly what AI contributed and what you did yourself.

⭐ Remember
  1. A strong pitch shows the problem, the solution and evidence that it works.
  2. A portfolio tells a learning story: drafts, tests and improvements.
  3. AI changes tasks, but knowledge, creativity and judgment stay human.
✏️ Quick review
  1. Why is a live demonstration stronger than a description?
  2. Choose one of your creations. What did AI contribute, and what did you check?
  3. Pick a job you like. Which tasks might AI change, and which stay human?
